A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
reconcile
Check that two sets of information agree.
chain of custody
The documented history of who held an item.
attribute
Identify who was responsible for something.
beneficiary
A person who receives support or money.
conservation
Careful protection of damaged documents.
proposition
A statement that evidence may support or reject.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The call from Fiona Bell came with the kind of news Emma had spent weeks trying not to anticipate. The trust's representatives and the storage contractor had conducted a supervised opening of the carton identified through the 2013 relocation index. They had reconciled the visible box labels as far as possible, documented the seal and prepared a preliminary contents inventory before examining the papers.

Among them was a bound volume headed “Student Travel — Authorisations 2011”. The title corresponded closely to the missing item on the trust's 2012 storage list, though Fiona insisted that its identity had yet to be established by comparing internal references. A plausible match was not an authenticated chain of custody.

Emma asked first about what the book recorded, not who might be implicated. Fiona described dated entries with reference fields and spaces for approval. Some contained initials or marks that could not yet be attributed reliably. Other fields were blank. The volume did not itself comprise bank-transfer confirmations, and the trust would not disclose information capable of identifying former applicants.

Sarah's reaction was immediate. “If Malcolm was the chair, perhaps those are his approvals.”

“Perhaps,” Emma answered, “but authority under a scheme and authorship of a particular mark are separate questions. And neither one establishes that money reached a beneficiary.”

Fiona subsequently provided a non-identifying inspection summary. At the front of the volume, a procedural note instructed administrators to cross-reference a later action when an exceptional case was resolved. The wording resembled the guidance already identified in the exceptions folder. This strengthened the case for comparing the two records, without demonstrating that the procedures had always been followed.

A loose leaf near the volume's centre required conservation advice before further handling. The inspectors had not established whether any page was absent, and Emma rejected Sarah's tentative suggestion that it had been deliberately removed. Physical deterioration, binding damage and interference were different explanations requiring different evidence.

Emma thought of Helen Ward's cousin. The privately examined letter had indicated selection conditional on further checks. It had neither established a completed transfer nor authorised the newsroom to search confidential foundation files for the applicant's identity. Nothing about the newly recovered book changed those limits.

She revised her evidence map into four propositions: an exception was recorded; approval was given; funds were transmitted; funds were received. The volume might clarify the first two, subject to authentication. The latter stages required independent accounting or banking evidence. The anonymous caller's earlier insistence on identifying approvers remained a lead, not proof of the caller's knowledge or motives.

By evening Fiona had reported one preliminary overlap: an entry in the volume used the same reference convention as the examples in the exceptions guidance. No particular payment, signatory or student had yet been matched. The team would compare dates and complete references before deciding what could be stated.

Emma closed her notes with an unfamiliar feeling. The investigation had at last produced a tangible object that might answer a precise question. But the difference between locating a book and verifying an allegation was exactly the difference she could no longer afford to ignore.

Before they ended the call, Emma asked whether Fiona could pass an invitation through a trusted intermediary. If Claire wished to speak, the newsroom could offer a private conversation without seeking her address. Fiona agreed to enquire, committing neither Claire to a response nor herself to disclosing how contact might be made.
